title: Mindful Trauma and Emotion Processing Methods (ATEM)-Study: Targeting stress reactivity in adults with Major Depression and histories of childhood maltreatment through Mindfulness-Based Stress Sensitivity Therapy (MBSST)
summary:
Depression is one of the leading causes of disease-related disability. More than half of people with depression have experienced abuse or neglect during childhood. These individuals often experience greater difficulties in dealing with stress, and existing treatments are often less effective for them than for other people.
The ATEM study aims to develop a treatment specifically for this group.
A total of 24 adults with depression and such childhood experiences will participate in Mindfulness-Based Stress Sensitivity Therapy (MBSST), divided into three groups. MBSST is a 12-week group therapy program with one session per week. Participants will also be given brief exercises to practice between sessions.
MBSST includes mindfulness exercises (practices that help people become more aware of their experiences in a calm, nonjudgmental way), as well as strategies for managing emotions, developing healthier behaviors, navigating relationships, and processing distressing childhood experiences. However, participants are not required to talk about these experiences.
To improve MBSST, we will ask participants before, during, and after the therapy how they are feeling and what they think about the group program. We will use their feedback to improve MBSST, with the long-term goal of developing an effective treatment for adults with depression who have experienced childhood abuse or neglect.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
•	At least moderate experiences of childhood maltreatment, defined by a score above the validated cut-off-value on at least one of the scales of the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ, Wingenfeld et al., 2010)
o	Physical neglect ≥ 10
o	Emotional neglect ≥ 15
o	Sexual abuse ≥ 8
o	Physical abuse ≥ 10
o	Emotional abuse ≥ 13
•	A primary diagnosis of major depression according to the DSM-5, determined using the Diagnostic Interview for Mental Disorders (DIPS-OA)
Exclusion criteria:
•	High risk for suicidal behaviour (active suicidal thought with at least partial intent) or a suicide attempt whin the last year; assessed using the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS; Posner et al., 2009)
•	Meeting the DSM-5 criteria for one or more of the following disorders (assessed using the Diagnostic Interview for Mental Disorders (DIPS-OA), unless stated otherwise)
o	Bipolar disorders
o	Current or lifetime psychotic disorders (if needed further assessment using the psychosis chapter of the strucutred clincial interview for DSM-5 - Clinician version [SCID-5-CV; Beesdo-Baum et al., 2019])
o	Eating disorders
o	Obsessive-compulsive disorders
o	Acute stress disorder
o	Current substance use disorder not in remission
o	Borderline personality disorder
•	Pregnancy (self-disclosure)
•	 Having started a psychotherapeutic, pharmacological or other treatment within the last three months
•	Regular meditation practice of at least 20 minutes at least twice weekly
•	Factors that, based on clinical judgment, are incompatible with safe or regular participation in group therapy. These include, in particular, currently stressful or unstable life circumstances (e.g., severe physical illness, ongoing contact with a perpetrator, or ongoing abuse), as well as insufficient psychological stability or inability to participate appropriately in group therapy, for example due to severe dissociative symptoms, frequent flashbacks involving loss of orientation to the present, or severe affective dysregulation.
Dissociative symptoms are assessed using the DIPS-OA and, if indicated, through additional assessment using the Questionnaire for Dissociative Symptoms (FDS). An FDS mean score ≥ 13 is considered an indicator of clinically relevant dissociative symptoms and is taken into account in the clinical assessment.
